title: Jenna Johnson on Her Rich ‘DWTS’ Legacy and How Season 35 Could Become Her “Dream Come True”
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 29, 2026 8:30am Jenna Johnson. Carly Sharp Logo text Jenna Johnson has had a fruitful career as a Dancing With the Stars professional dancer. Season 35 with Harry Shum Jr. is shaping up to be another standout season on her résumé. “You know when you look around and you’re like, Oh, I’m exactly where I need to be ? That’s how our partnership feels,” the pro tells The Hollywood Reporter of her collaboration with the actor. “I feel so grateful this partnership happened. That’s the beauty of casting — we have no control over it, but once you’re in that pairing, you realize like, This was meant to be .” Related Stories TV Tamera Mowry-Housley Boards 'Scrubs' Season 2 TV Philo Sets Exclusive Streaming Date for Page Six 'Virtual Reali-Tea Awards' The Emmy-nominated choreographer has won DWTS twice, and could become the most decorated female pro if she won her third mirrorball this year. She’d also tie the record for the second-most wins ever for a pro, evening out with Mark Ballas and her husband Val Chmerkovskiy, who each have three wins. Those are statistics she did not know, and she doesn’t want to think about right now. “I really just want to focus on one week at a time ( Laughs ). But those are incredible facts,” she says, although it’s a reality Jenna could soon face if she and Harry make it to the season 35 finale this fall. Below, Jenna dishes on how So You Think You Could Dance led her to DWTS ; reflects on her niece, Hailey Bills, following in her footsteps being partnered with a woman on the show; what Pasha Pashkov really told her during that internet-breaking Viral Hits Night moment ; and her Broadway aspirations. *** It’s my understanding you were noticed on So You Think You Could Dance and then brought into the DWTS troupe. I also know you come from the interconnected world that is the Utah ballroom dance scene, so can you talk about your journey to getting on the troupe? I did grow up in Utah at the same studio that a lot of the pros grew up at. I was a competitive Latin dancer as well as in the commercial convention circuit for jazz, ballet and hip hop. At the time, So You Think You Can Dance was popping, so I auditioned and I got onto it, which was absolutely incredible. It’s pretty ironic, but So You Think You Can Dance and Dancing With the Stars are filmed at the same studio at CBS Television City, and I guess the producers caught wind of my name, and they asked me to be on the troupe. Growing up at my studio in Utah, I had seen people like Derek and Julianne make it in L.A.; they’re dancing for their careers, and they’re household names as ballroom dancers. It was iconic, so to be asked to join the troupe, I was so hungry and eager to learn as much as I could. At that time I joined, you still had the OG pros on the show. There was Derek, Karina [Smirnoff], Kym Johnson, Maks [Chmerkovskiy], Tony Devolani; it was OG pros that I got to really watch their process and learn from. I’m so grateful for that time period because it gave me the tools to go into my time as a pro and feel like I could have the confidence to navigate it. Your first season as a pro, you were eliminated first, then you took a break for season 24 and came back for season 25 and w o n with Adam [Rippon]. How do you reflect back on your early time on the show? I think timing is everything, and everything happens for a reason. I kind of got to experience this with my niece [Hailey Bills] just barely; she was eliminated her first season as a pro [this season], but there’s such a beautiful journey that’s awaiting you. It was very unique being eliminated my first season, but then getting to be partnered with someone like Adam Rippon the next season and take home a mirrorball; to feel that sensation is one of the craziest moments of my life. But I think that’s the beauty of the show, is getting to be partnered with somebody so vastly different each year. Can you take me through that moment when you learned Hailey was going to be a pro this season? I hate to say this, but I wasn’t surprised, because she is one of the most talented human beings I know. I think she really made a name for herself the first year on troupe; she just has that star quality. Obviously, I wanted it for her, and I know how much she wanted it and how much it meant to her. So when she did get asked to be a pro, it just made sense. I can’t wait to see what she does as a pro on the show. Her journey was cut short this year, but man, it is just getting started for her. I can’t wait to see what she does next in the next upcoming season. Her casting was also monumental in the fact that she was the second pro to be in an all-female partnership, second to obviously you. Do you think the decision to pair Hailey with another woman was at all a callback to your partnership with JoJo Siwa or was done in a way where you could guide her in this second-of-a-kind casting for Dancing With the Stars ? You know, I’m not sure why, but I do think that it made sense: the casting of [Hailey and Sarah Jane Nader] together. They were both young, they looked absolutely stunning next to each other, and their personalities were super fun and playful together. I think that the casting was brilliant, and it made sense. Is it ironic that the two of us are the ones to do it? Absolutely. When she was told that she’d be dancing with a female, I wanted to do that for her, because I have been in that situation before, so anything she needed, I wanted to help her out in any way. It is pretty crazy. Like, we’ll always have that bond that we can share together. There is so much discourse going into new seasons about who is partnered with who, and [your season 35 partner] Harry is obviously an amazing dancer. What would you say to somebody who is critical of pros being partnered with “ringers”? What is your take on that discourse? It happens every year, so I think we can expect it. But I think they do need to know that we have nothing to do with our casting. That is not our decision whatsoever. It’s very much up to the production of it all, and they have a rhyme and a reason for all of the pairings. So when there is discourse and there are lots of loud opinions, [I] totally get everyone having their feelings. But there’s nothing we can do. We are given our partner, and then from then on, it is our responsibility to show up and be there for them. So I understand when there is a lot of talk, and obviously there was this current season. But I’m just doing my job. I’m doing what I’m told. And ringer or not, I think each partnership is going to bring its own challenges. With this quote-unquote “ringer” title, that’s a lot of pressure to live up to. Plus, I’ll just speak for my partnership on behalf of Harry, even though he has some dance experience — yes, we’re not running away from that. But dance is so vastly different. He’s never done Latin. He’s never done ballroom. He’s never done frame. All of this is a new world for him, so I hope people can appreciate the effort and hard work that he does put in because that shouldn’t go unnoticed. Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson on Dancing With the Stars season 35. Disney/Christopher Willard As a viewer, it appears that you and Harry have such similar energies. How has working with him so far this season been? Honestly, literally, since the first day we met, there have been so many synchronicities in our lives. You know when you look around and you’re like, Oh, I’m exactly where I need to be ? That’s how our partnership feels. It’s wild to think that I didn’t know him a couple weeks or months ago, because he just fit so beautifully into my life. It’s been so much fun being paired with him, and I feel so grateful this partnership happened. That’s the beauty of casting — we have no control over it, but once you’re in that pairing, you realize like, This was meant to be . This upcoming week is Yacht Rock Night. What do you have planned for that number with Harry? I’m so excited because we’re doing Jive to a great Hall & Oates song, and it feels very Harry. He’s the epitome of joy and bubbly energy, and that’s what we want to do this week. We just want to put a smile on people’s faces. Jive is one of my favorite styles to do because it’s upbeat and fast, but you want to get up and dance with someone. On last Tuesday night’s episode, there was a clip of you and Pasha after Maura Higgins’ dance that went viral. Everybody was trying to figure out what Pasha said to you. Are you able to share what happened in that conversation? Of course. So before Maura and Mark had come up, we were actually just raving about what an incredible dancer Maura is, and Pasha was telling me while they were talking, and this is kind of what went viral, but he was saying, “I saw them do the cha-cha in the beginning of the week.” I guess he had come in and watched their dance early on in the week, and he was like, “It is incredible, her improvement, she’s just gotten so much better” from that first initial rehearsal that he saw. And so you see me going like, “Wow, that’s awesome.” ( Laughs ) So that’s what he was telling me, and everyone was like, “What are they saying?” But we were really just [going] goo-goo ga-ga about how much we love Maura. That’s the tea. This could be the first year that you and your husband, Val, potentially make a finale together. What would that experience mean to you? There’s so much that can happen from now until then, but I would absolutely love to have that moment together. It’s kind of funny, for the past 10 years that we’ve been competing on the show against one another, we’ve never had a situation where both of us have two capable people. It’s like either one of us is going to the finale, the other one’s eliminated early, or vice versa. So this [year on season 35] was a really unique experience for us navigating it. I’m just always so grateful for his support, and I love cheering him on. It’s one of my favorite things to do in the ballroom, so to be able to share that special moment together would be a dream come true, obviously. We will see what happens. You’re very immersed in Dancing With the Stars right now. What do you see yourself doing next? Would you ever potentially do any other competitive reality TV shows? I really wanted to do Special Forces . I love physical activity, so I feel like that would be fun. Other than that, regarding reality shows, I really just want to be a judge on a baking show. Like, that is my dream, honestly. That’s as dramatic as I want to get in the reality space. But career-wise, I feel so blessed that I get to do my dream job every day. I don’t take that for granted. I would really love to dabble in Broadway. I would love to experience live theater in that sort of a situation. But also, I really love my mentor, Mandy Moore. She has just changed the way that dance has been portrayed in films and in TV shows, so I would love to also really dive into choreography of it all and putting it more into film and TV. I saw a video you posted right before the season started: Y’all were in New York and you were talking about how Broadway was something you wanted to do. Have you heard from anybody from that world yet? I absolutely geeked out because the premiere night there was a producer from Chicago in the audience, and I was just like, What is life right now? That was pretty epic. Jenna Johnson. Carly Sharp What is your favorite part of a full week in the Dancing With the Stars process: choreography, teaching/rehearsing, dress rehearsal or live show day? I really think it’s the rehearsal process. I love watching somebody put in hard work and effort, and seeing it come to fruition. I’m just going to speak on my partner right now, but watching Harry have no ego in the midst of learning something new, that is so fulfilling as a partner, as a choreographer. I think it’s really beautiful, this concept of shared purpose. We go into rehearsal having a combined goal, and to be able to achieve that together of like, “OK, today, let’s focus on getting the routine to count; tomorrow, let’s focus on getting it to music; now let’s add in the performance element,” I love that camaraderie of having a partner that you accomplish goals with and have a shared intention and purpose. I obviously also love the creation of it, although we’re kind of always on a time constraint during the season. That can be a little bit stressful. But I think watching somebody do something scary, put in their whole heart and soul, and effort, blood, sweat and tears and then watching them accomplish it is the best part. What is your favorite style of dance to choreograph? I really love a Tango. It’s the best; it’s sharp, strong, hot, sexy. There’s so much traveling, there’s a lot of power behind it. But also, this week, I’m having so much fun with the jive Do you have a favorite number that you have choreographed on Dancing With the Stars ? Oh man, that’s so hard. That’s like asking to pick your favorite child. One that stands out forever will be the piece that Val and I got to choreograph for Len Goodman, for his tribute . That was one of the most special creations of my life, and to honor somebody who holds so much legacy, it was really special. I also do have to say my dance that I did with Joey [Graziadei] to give up our title — each time somebody wins, they come back the next season and do an honor dance in the finale. The dance that Joey and I got to do last year in the [season 34] finale was one of my top favorite dances ever, ever, ever. Describe Dancing With the Stars season 35 in one word. Mind-blowing. *** Season 35 of DWTS airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m., simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, and streaming the next day on Hulu. Read all of THR ‘s DWTS coverage here . THR

title: JioStar’s Kevin Vaz Urges Indian Government to Restore BARC TV Audience Ratings as Media Sector Hits $28.9 Billion
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 8:24am PT JioStar’s Kevin Vaz Urges Indian Government to Restore BARC TV Audience Ratings as Media Sector Hits $28.9 Billion By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Tops U.K., Ireland Box Office 12 hours ago ‘Hirayasumi’ Anime Unveils Footage, Key Visual and Lead Voice Cast Ahead of NHK Debut 15 hours ago Mohammad Rasoulof, O Mipo to Receive Tokyo Film Festival’s Kurosawa Akira Award 16 hours ago See All FICCI Frames Leading Indian streamer JioStar ‘s Kevin Vaz has called on India’s government to immediately restore BARC audience ratings, using the inaugural address at the FICCI-Frames conference to warn that the data gap is leaving broadcasters, advertisers and agencies without dependable numbers heading into the festive season. Vaz is the CEO of entertainment at JioStar and chair of the FICCI Media & Entertainment Committee. He thanked India’s Ministry of Information & Broadcasting for scrapping the 10+2 advertising cap, describing the move as a step toward rules that fit how linear TV and the wider media business now operate. Related Stories Glen Basner Says FilmNation Will Ramp Up Slate in 2027, Is Ready to ‘Raise His Fist’ for ‘I Play Rocky’ and Celebrate ‘Thoughtful’ and ‘Entertaining’ ‘Bunker’ Martin McDonagh Jokes About His Past – as a Hitman – and Calls ‘Wild Horse Nine’ His Most Political Film: ‘There’s Too Much Artistic Neutrality and Too Much Saying Nothing’ The ministry first ordered BARC to stop publishing news channel ratings on March 6, citing sensationalist coverage of the Israel-Iran conflict, and extended that pause several times. In early July, it widened the freeze to all genres until BARC secures registration under the Television Ratings Policy 2026, which took effect in March. BARC applied on April 29 and has expanded its panel to 70,876 homes against the policy’s 80,000-home target, but ratings remain suspended. Popular on Variety “At a time of global economic uncertainty, reliable audience measurement is critical to keeping this ecosystem efficient, supporting advertisers and broadcasters, and keeping domestic economic activity moving,” Vaz said. He also pressed for a concrete roadmap to strip away the regulatory load and costs that weigh on linear broadcasting. Forbearance has been a long-standing demand from the sector, he said, and self-regulation backed by solid industry standards should sit at the core of its next phase. The appeal comes as the sector continues to grow. Indian media and entertainment expanded 9% in 2025 to INR2.78 trillion ($28.9 billion), Vaz said. Digital passed INR1.1 trillion ($11.5 billion), while live events jumped 47%. Through much of its history, Vaz said, the hard limit on Indian media was distribution, with too few channels and screens for stories to reach viewers. “Attention is the new currency, and in an era where content and ideas seem endless, the magic lies in creating something that makes the ‘thumb stop!'” he said. He pointed to Connected TV as a case where older and newer screens are converging rather than displacing each other. Citing industry estimates, Vaz put India’s CTV audience at more than 200 million viewers, with over 80% of that viewing done together with family or friends. Linear TV streaming, he added, lets viewers watch live channels on any screen and connection while opening up new options for measurement and advertising. The 2026 Indian Premier League (IPL) cricket tournament, which reached more than 1.2 billion viewers, was “perhaps the clearest expression” of that convergence, he said. Microdrama was worth INR6.5 billion ($68 million) in 2025, and the category is expected to grow at more than 50% a year by 2028, Vaz said. JioStar has entered the format through Tadka and is working with over 50 production houses, which he said was helping to bring more creators into the business. JioHotstar also let viewers find and buy products inside the app while they watched the IPL and a live stream of blockbuster “Dhurandhar The Revenge.” Vaz called content commerce a third “value pool” for the industry, next to advertising and subscriptions. On AI, Vaz said the technology is reshaping production, storytelling, workflows, analytics and personalization. “But even as technology expands what is possible, the human being must remain at the center of the creative ecosystem,” he said. He called for clear rules on copyright, consent, attribution and a fair return for creators, so that technology and creativity move forward together. Before turning to the industry’s numbers, Vaz asked the room to pause in silence for the late Leena Jaisani, FICCI’s deputy secretary general and head of media and entertainment, who helped found its Media & Entertainment Committee. This year’s edition, held under the theme “India’s Media Moment: Creating Value in an Age of Infinite Content,” marks 26 years of the committee’s work through FICCI Frames. Vaz closed by urging the industry to judge itself on the value it creates rather than on output or reach. “Did we build intellectual property that could travel from India to the world?” he asked. title: Sky Confirms Plans To Showcase Series Like ‘The Day Of The Jackal’ On ITV After Takeover
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jake Kanter Jake Kanter International Investigations Editor @Jake_Kanter More Stories By Jake Jeremy Clarkson Working On “Unbelievably Ambitious” Show Amid Uncertainty Over ‘Clarkson’s Farm’ Future Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra Open To Putting Shows On BBC iPlayer — Just Don’t Mention A Merger Sony Chief Wayne Garvie: “It’s Very Difficult To See How Channel 4 Survives In Present Form” View All September 29, 2026 8:23am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'The Day of the Jackal' SkyShowtime The Day of the Jackal and Brassic could be coming to free-to-air television in the UK after Sky completes its £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) takeover of ITV ‘s network operations. Cécile Frot-Coutaz, Sky’s content chief and the CEO of Sky Studios , has said that the Comcast-owned company wants to experiment with windowing its original series on ITV over the coming years. Frot-Coutaz’s comments, which were made at the Royal Television Society London Convention on Tuesday, confirm Deadline’s report in July about Sky’s plans to give original series airtime on its new asset . Related Stories News Sister Boss Predicts "Premium" TV Talent & Drama Will "End Up On YouTube Or TikTok" News Jeremy Clarkson Working On "Unbelievably Ambitious" Show Amid Uncertainty Over 'Clarkson's Farm' Future Frot-Coutaz said Sky would look at showcasing old seasons of a show like The Day of the Jackal on ITV ahead of a new season launching. “There’s various permutations,” she said. Watch on Deadline The former Fremantle executive said Sky previously experimented with a similar windowing strategy when it put the first four seasons of Brassic on Netflix. “We saw that we had been able to find some new headroom [in viewing] because we’d exposed the show to an audience that we didn’t have,” she said. Frot-Coutaz added that Sky will also look closely at putting sport on ITV, opening up the possibility that Premier League football could get free-to-air exposure. She explained: “We have 40,000 hours of sports. So within that, there’s also huge opportunities in terms of putting more sports on free-to-air. We think everybody wins from that. The viewer wins, but also the leagues win.” Earlier in the day, ITV CEO Carolyn McCall said the company had little choice but to sell to Sky because the “competition is ferocious.” As part of the takeover, Sky has agreed a £2.1 billion output deal with ITV Studios, which will guarantee that shows like Love Island and Coronation Street will remain on ITV until 2032. Asked if Sky could rip up this deal in six years, McCall responded: “Good luck.” She added that, if anything, Sky will start commissioning more from ITV Studios, which will remain independent and listed on the London Stock Exchange. title: Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 8:22am PT Sylvester Stallone Says Superhero Movie Bodies Aren’t ‘Natural’ and Taking Steroids to Bulk Up Is Like ‘Putting on Part of a Costume’ By Antonio Ferme Plus Icon Antonio Ferme Latest Chris Rock Says Infidelity and Struggling to ‘Make It’ Aren’t Just Hollywood Problems: ‘If You Got No Love, You’re Broke as F—k’ 2 days ago ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Sets Sights on Best Picture Oscar Nomination: ‘If the Possibility Is Not Zero, It’s Hard Not to Have a Little Bit of Hope’ 2 days ago ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Champions Franchise’s First R Rating as Sequel Rocks NYFF at World Premiere: ‘Censoring’ the Action ‘Was Not an Option’ 3 days ago See All Getty Images Sylvester Stallone is sharing the story of how “ Rocky ” got made 50 years after its release in his new tell-all memoir, “Steps,” which hits shelves today. Part of the Oscar winner’s press tour brought him to New York 92nd Street Y for a 50-minute conversation with journalist Tracy Smith about his early career struggles, the legacy of the “Rocky” franchise and the physical toll of his action roles. After making headlines for telling The New York Times that he was “bulimic” while filming “Rocky III” and discussing the “terrible toll” steroids took on his body, Stallone explained to Smith that he rationalized his drug use with his desire to push the Rocky Balboa character in a new direction. Related Stories 'Obsession,' 'Backrooms' Ushering in Shift Similar to 'Easy Rider' in 1970s, Sony Pictures Classics Co-Chief Says Matthew McConaughey Exposed Himself to Jimmy Kimmel in the Emmys Bathroom and Woody Harrelson Saw the Whole Thing “By the time they did ‘Rocky III,’ you’ve lost the element of surprise. Everyone knows what this guy is all about,” Stallone said. “I wanted him to develop serious narcissism. I wanted him to get his scars removed and be a totally different guy. That would be a story point. He became protected, he’s shielded and vain. And when he finally met Mr. T, or Clubber Lang, that’s where reality hit him. But to do that, I had to do a total body metamorphosis. So I went from like 50% body fat to 2.6%. I did it literally by eating tuna fish and [drinking] maybe 30 cups of coffee a day. And, of course, there’s steroids.” Popular on Variety When the audience responded with audible gasps, Stallone made light of the fact that he’s hardly the first and only Hollywood action star to use steroids and go to extreme lengths to achieve a certain bulked-up physique. “Guys … you really think these guys are natural?” Stallone quipped. “If you’re trying to play a sort of superhero or a person that is above and beyond a normal guy, you can’t do it. It’s almost like putting on part of a costume. For six to eight weeks, you manifest that book. And then you shed it.” When Smith asked when Stallone realized he could no longer continue using steroids and maintaining such an arduous workout routine, the actor recalled experiencing “a wake-up call” after having a heart valve replaced. His wife, Jennifer Flavin Stallone, insisted he get checked out after he appeared unwell. Stallone believes the examination “absolutely” saved his life. “And I thought I was okay. I was lucky that my wife said, ‘I don’t like the way you look.’ [I said], ‘Oh, come on. I’m just getting old over here. Relax,’” he recalled. “Women have an extra sense. They really do.” The live interview with Stallone marked the first installment of “ CBS Sunday Morning at 92NY,” a new series of conversations featuring prominent figures from the worlds of arts, politics and culture before a live audience. The series serves as an extension of “CBS Sunday Morning,” the network’s long-running Sunday morning news program. “For over 150 years, the 92nd Street Y has been a world-class beacon for culture, deep conversation and intellectual curiosity,” said 92NY CEO Seth Pinsky. “We are honored to work with ‘CBS Sunday Morning’ on this incredible new programming series. By bringing two great American institutions together, we are creating the kind of deeply engaging experiences our communities crave and expect.” Stallone and Smith’s live conversation will begin streaming on CBSSundayMorning.com, YouTube and Paramount+ later this week. title: Steven Knight on Making the Leap From ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ to ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ to, Eventually, James Bond
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 8:08am PT Steven Knight on Making the Leap From ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?’ to ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ to, Eventually, James Bond By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest Daniel Webber, Dermot Mulroney and Katheryn Winnick to Lead Psychological Thriller ‘Compound 9’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago Jeremy Clarkson Is Already Thinking About What Comes After ‘Clarkson’s Farm’: ‘It Has to Be Unbelievably Ambitious’ 3 hours ago Should the BBC and Channel 4 Merge? Sony Pictures Television’s International Production Boss Wayne Garvie Thinks So 5 hours ago See All Getty Images One of the most prolific writers and creators working today, Steven Knight ‘s body of work includes the likes of “Peaky Blinders,” “SAS: Rogue Heroes,” “House of Guinness,” “A Thousand Blows” and, most famously (even though it’s not even started filming), the next James Bond film. But, as many might not be aware, his first major breakthrough in the industry was as one of the creators of global smash hit TV game show “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” in the late 1990s. Related Stories 'Avengers: Doomsday' Star Alan Cumming Says 'I Don't Fully Understand the Plot' and Only Acted With Florence Pugh's Stunt Double ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Co-Director Explains It’s ‘Very Difficult’ to Evolve Marvel Characters, but ‘We Need to Surprise Ourselves’ and ‘Audiences’ This seemingly wild shift from quiz show phenomenons to hit dramas was discussed in a special conversation with Knight at the RTS London Convention on Tuesday, where he revealed that his secret at the time was having “two computers.” Popular on Variety While “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” was starting to make a splash, Knight said he was also writing radio and radio commercials, writing comedy for stand-ups (including British icons such as Frankie Howard, Ken Dodd and Jasper Carrot), and also writing novels. “I’d had a couple of novels published, and at the time of ‘Millionaire’ I was writing a fourth novel, and it was going to be ‘Dirty Pretty Things,'” he said. “It was going to be a novel, but I was writing it in present tense, which is how you write a script. So I thought, ‘Well, I might as well do the script.” That script wound up getting into the hands of Stephen Frears and turned into the acclaimed 2002 film starring Chiwetel Ejiofor and Audrey Tautou. “And then I was in. I went to Hollywood on the back of that,” Knight said, but noted that he was still “introduced in every meeting I went to as the man who helped make ‘Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?” Nearly a quarter-century on and Knight is one of the most in-demand writers around, having recently been hired by Noel and Liam Gallagher to shape the Oasis tour documentary “Don’t Look Back in Anger” and by Amazon MGM to pen the long-awaited 26th James Bond film and 007 franchise reboot. While Bond wasn’t outwardly discussed in Knight’s RTS talk, it was referenced as “the unmentionable thing,” with host Gaby Roslin asking him if it felt like a “heavy weight” on his shoulder. “Not at all…. title: How Britney Spears and the ‘Cannibal Cop’ Left Erin Lee Carr Forever Changed
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 8:00am PT How Britney Spears and the ‘Cannibal Cop’ Left Erin Lee Carr Forever Changed By Marlow Stern Plus Icon Marlow Stern Chief Correspondent Latest How Britney Spears and the ‘Cannibal Cop’ Left Erin Lee Carr Forever Changed 33 minutes ago Mayor Zohran Mamdani Refuses Jimmy Kimmel’s Request to Text Trump a Selfie of Them 11 hours ago John Cho’s Odyssey From ‘MILF Guy #2’ to Porn-Hating Pastor in ‘Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’: ‘It Felt Very Lonesome at Times’ 4 days ago See All Getty Images/Netflix/Tribeca Few documentary filmmakers are as prolific as Erin Lee Carr . In the last five years alone, the in-demand director has helmed the controversial Netflix doc “Britney vs Spears,” “The Ringleader: The Case of the Bling Ring,” “Fanatical: The Catfishing of Tegan and Sara,” the docuseries “I Am Not a Monster: The Lois Riess Murders” and scripted series “Murdaugh: Death in the Family.” She’s also produced “Stormy,” a doc on embattled Trump accuser Stormy Daniels , “Trophy Wife: Murder on Safari” and “Perfect Wife: The Mysterious Disappearance of Sherri Papini.” If you see a throughline there — centering the stories of women — that is by design, and something Carr chalks up to a terrifying encounter with the “ Cannibal Cop ” Gilberto Valle, the subject of her 2015 film “Thought Crimes: The Case of the Cannibal Cop,” that turned her world upside down (more on that later). Related Stories Tilly Norwood Creator Says AI Actress Made 'Many People Realize That AI Is Coming' and 'That Was the Point' Glen Basner Says FilmNation Will Ramp Up Slate in 2027, Is Ready to ‘Raise His Fist’ for ‘I Play Rocky’ and Celebrate ‘Thoughtful’ and ‘Entertaining’ ‘Bunker’ Her latest is “The Swan: Behind the Mirror.” Premiering Sept. 29 on Hulu, the feature-length documentary explores Nely Galán’s notorious 2004 Fox reality-competition series “ The Swan ,” where 16 women — so-called “ugly ducklings” — subjected themselves to extreme plastic surgery, dentistry, training, dieting and a little bit of therapy to transform themselves into what a panel of experts deemed more “attractive” versions of themselves. They would then compete against one another in a beauty pageant, which had a lingerie portion for God knows what reason, for the ultimate prize of being crowned The Swan. It is considered one of the worst reality TV shows ever produced, and the doc features eye-opening testimonials for a dozen former contestants, many of whom were left traumatized by the experience , as well as series producers and even one of its plastic surgeons, who comes off particularly bad. Popular on Variety “On a personal level, I didn’t like my body and what I looked like and always wanted to look like somebody else,” Carr tells Variety about making the doc. “But in many ways, ‘The Swan’ was a harbinger of what was to come.” Carr, 38, is the daughter of late, great New York Times columnist David Carr, and managed to find a window in her packed schedule to fit in “The Swan: Behind the Mirror,” nestling it between “a feature for Netflix that I’m going to finish in the next couple of months” and some more “scripted things” she’s cooking up. But for now, we’re here to talk about “The Swan” — and her “ Britney vs Spears ” ordeal. Did you watch “The Swan” when it was on TV? I wasn’t allowed to watch TV on the weekdays — my father was very intense — but I ended up sneaking it and found out about the show. At the time, I was a huge Britney Spears person and I was like, OK, what am I trying to look like? I just remember seeing a clip of this really intense dentistry and plastic surgery that haunted me, and I don’t think I watched the rest of the show. When Hulu contacted me saying that Expectation TV, this U.K. production company, had this I was like, I gotta do it! I didn’t even have room in my schedule but figured it out. How long did the process take to make “The Swan: Behind the Mirror?” I was not given a lot of time. I will say it was under a year. Typically, the films that I make take 18 months, and I do it to protect the editorial process and develop access in a way that feels deeply meaningful. In this case, a lot of the access had been figured out. Some of the Swans were onboard, Dr. Terry [Dubrow] was a maybe, Dr. Haworth was a maybe, Nely [Galán] I’d had many conversations with. What I immediately knew at the beginning was: I’m not going to cast inside this documentary. Typically, you pick three people and that’s all a feature has room for; you don’t have 12 participants. But I wasn’t going to do the same thing that happened to these women where they got chosen whose story was best. I needed to interview everyone for 2-3 hours and we’d figure it out in the edit. What happened with trying to convince Terry Dubrow and Nely Galán to be in the doc? I’ll let you in on a little secret: Terry wanted a sum of money that would never make sense for a documentary expert. It was under $100,000 for one interview. And with Nely, it’s her show and it’s her footage so if anyone was going to do a “Swan” documentary, it was going to be her. Plus, she wanted to be an executive producer on it and that wasn’t going to work. So then we were in discussions about licensing the footage and we did not end up licensing the footage — it was fair use, so that had to be carefully constructed. When you see the iPad inside the interview scenes it was because they had to comment on the parts of the show. How do you feel about the Terry Dubrow of it all, who now features on “The Real Housewives of Orange County?” He’s had some harsh comments about the women who’ve expressed sadness over appearing on “The Swan.” He said it was “all a bunch of BS,” and I wrote back to him, and I was like, “I’m excited to hear what you think.” I think he’s a reasonable and rational man, and when he sees this, he’ll understand. Maybe his recollection was that he helped people, but that’s not the case. And I was actually really surprised that he was dismissing the experiences of the women so publicly. When I looked into the women and their time on the show, Dr. Dubrow was very well-liked. So, I think it’s puzzling that that is the stance he would take before even watching [the film]. One of the more startling revelations in the documentary concerns a nude photo shoot Dr. Haworth subjected the Season 2 contestants to that seemed incredibly sketchy. He ended up giving the photos to production to give back to the women, but there would be no agreement about deleting or destroying the photos. He said it was for an “art book” and I think the story checked out that it actually was for that, but the circumstances of the women not knowing why they were taking these photos and the fact that production people weren’t at the photo shoot, in a story about exploitation it’s important to include those details. There seemed to be a turning point in your career about a decade ago where you really started focusing on women’s stories. What changed? Do you want to know the craziest reason why that happened? I did “Thought Crimes: The Case of the Cannibal Cop,” and my male subject [Gilberto Valle] would not stop messaging me. I felt harassed and stalked, and I said, I’m never making a film about a man again . I’m not going to fear for my physical safety, I care about women and I’m a long-term feminist. I even advocated for Gil Valle in my film that it had been thought crimes! I ultimately found my path but it’s because this early thing happened to me. I later met an FBI officer in Manhattan who was like, “That guy was absolutely going to kill people so you shouldn’t live where you live.” So you moved because of the “Cannibal Cop?” Because of the “Cannibal Cop” and I had to move in with a cutie in Astoria. Another prominent documentary filmmaker, Alex Gibney, is dealing with legal threats right now from the richest man in the world over his “Musk” doc. How worried are you about legal risk? It’s a scary time to be a documentary filmmaker when it comes to legal risk. I did the “Stormy” film with Sarah Gibson and Judd Apatow, and there was Trump legal risk associated with it. Who I am before that and who I am after makes me feel differently about risk. They tried to file an injunction, the Southern District of New York didn’t want the film coming out, we got legal letters while we were making it and it was a painful experience on all sides. I also got legal letters while I was making the Britney Spears doc and pressure from somebody at an agency saying not to do it. And Stormy Daniels lives as a hunted person. We premiered the film at South by Southwest and there had to be a bomb sweep before the film by security. So, all the hats I have off to Alex Gibney for saying, “I’m going to take on the richest and most litigious person in the world.” You mentioned your Britney Spears doc “Britney vs Spears,” and it did receive a good amount of pushback. There were critics who found it exploitive. Yes. I would say the Britney Spears thing was a very punishing experience in my life because I spent two years where every single moment of my life was dedicated to this person and trying to get her out of this unlawful conservatorship. Ultimately, she disavowed the film and said that people were exploiting her. There were very intense tactics taken by the filmmaking team to not do that. There was no showing of those photos that every doc that’s ever been about her has shown of the incident with the umbrella and her own mental health crisis. So, what I decided was: What other people think of my work can’t be a part of my opinion because then it will ruin how I make films. A part of me was extremely hurt by the process and the accusations, and it was dark days. Now, when I think about the work I am making and want to make, it’s about enthusiastic participation — people who want to do this and want their story to be out. That has been extremely healing for me as it relates to doing this with Hulu and the Swans. But Britney Spears is out of the conservatorship. Certain people think Britney’s not doing well, but she’s not being financially taken advantage of by her father anymore, so that’s a win. Given the work that you do now shining a light on women’s stories, how do you feel about starting your filmmaking career at a place like Vice that had an awful culture when it came to its treatment of women? I was a very strange kid in a bedroom shooting things that no one saw, and then I was a strange kid at an organization shooting things that people saw. I got to have a launchpad to my career. I made this film called “Click. Print. Gun.” about a guy who was printing AR-15s, and that got Andrew Rossi to notice me, and then I got into a room with Sheila Nevins. Would I be here sitting and talking to you and making films about the empowerment of women if that didn’t happen? No. Is it lost on me that the themes and values that I hold dear are incongruent [with Vice]? During one of the last fights I had with my father before he died, he said, “You are incredibly ungrateful when it comes to Vice. They made you a part of who you are.” He ended up really liking Vice. And I said, “Try being a woman working there.” We couldn’t see eye to eye on that. title: ‘The Love Hypothesis’ Author Ali Hazelwood to Release Book Sequel, MRC Developing Film for Amazon MGM
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All September 29, 2026 7:52am 'The Love Hypothesis' Philippe Bosse/Prime Video The story of Olive Smith and Adam Carlsen will continue in a book sequel. Author Ali Hazelwood announced Tuesday that she will release a sequel, The Two-Body Problem next February. The sequel is in early development and comes amid the recent release of Prime Video‘s adaptation of Hazelwood‘s bestseller The Love Hypothesis , starring Lili Reinhart and Tom Bateman. Sharing the cover on her social media Hazelwood wrote, “‘I wrote a sequel to The Love Hypothesis ‘ is not a sentence I thought I’d say a year or so ago, but now I weirdly can’t imagine a world in which The Two-Body Problem doesn’t exist. I’m really eager to talk more about this book and how it came about in the next few months. For now let me just say that the TLH movie and its cast made me fall for Adam and Olive all over again, that revisiting them was an absolute pleasure.“ Related Stories Lifestyle Kyle MacLachlan, Star of David Lynch's 'Dune,' Was the Only One on Set Who Knew What 'Dune' Was About TV Hints of 'Sex and the City' and 'Narcos': A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria She continued, “As someone who gets VERY attached to stories and characters, I know that unannounced sequels can be blindsiding, so feel free to skip this book and overwrite it with whatever headcanon you prefer, and I’ll see you on the next one! But if you want to read more about Adam and Olive, The Two-Body Problem spans a couple of years, and it’s a mix of slice of life, postdoctoral turmoil, and unflinching exploration of the hardest challenge one will face in a long-term relationship: deciding what to have for dinner. If you pick it up, I really hope you enjoy.“ Though she prefaced that “nothing is guaranteed,“ Hazelwood also announced, “MRC is developing a film based on the The Two-Body Problem for Amazon MGM Studios.“ Further details were not shared. Since its publication in 2021, The Love Hypothesis has since become a full-blown phenomenon — a New York Times bestseller, a BookTok obsession and a career launchpad, turning Hazelwood into a household name. Her books have sold more than 10 million copies worldwide, several already in the book-to-screen pipeline. The film adaptation, which premiered on Sept. 23 on Prime Video, was directed by Claire Scanlon and produced by Elizabeth Cantillon. The romance , which began as Star Wars ’ Reylo fan fiction (featuring Daisy Ridley’s Rey and Adam Driver’s Kylo Ren ) , follows Olive Smith ( Reinhart ), a graduate student and Stanford Ph.D. candidate who embarks on a fake romance with the notoriously stern Adam Carlsen ( Bateman ), known as “Dr. Evil” to his students. The move is solely to reassure her friend Anh (Rachel Marsh) that Olive’s feelings for her bestie’s current love interest are entirely behind her. The Two-Body Problem book will be published on Feb. 2, 2027. View this post on Instagram THR

title: ‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 7:45am PT ‘Sin Filtro’ Producer JK Media Producing First Original Microdramas Shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘The Platform’ Co-Producer David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment Spain Boards Matías Rojas’ ‘Dog Legs’ (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago Madrid Audiovisual Cluster Dives Deeper Into New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies at Iberseries & Platino Industria 10 hours ago See All Fernanda Romero in 'Trapped with the Enemy' Courtesy of JK Media JK Media, the producer behind the hit unscripted celebrity show “ Sin Filtro ” and its various iterations, has developed and produced the first original microdramas in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision ’s ViXMicrO. The new Spanish-language microdramas, “Trapped with the Enemy” (“Encerrada con el enemigo) and “Threatened Infidelity” (“Infidelidad amenazada”), were both shot in Los Angeles and are slated to bow in October this year. Each series consists of 60 episodes running 90 seconds each and will be available in Mexico and the U.S. Related Stories Zurich Film Festival Heads on Theatrical-Loving Gen Z, Prioritizing Private Equity and Tilly Norwood a Year Later: This Is the ‘Place Where You Address the Real Hot Questions’ Tilly Norwood Creator Says AI Actress Made 'Many People Realize That AI Is Coming' and 'That Was the Point' “We are excited to dive into the microdrama space for the first time and launching some of the first-ever U.S. produced vertical series for ViXMicrO,” said JK Media Group founder and CEO Sebastian Jimenez. Popular on Variety JK Media Group founder and CEO Sebastian Jimenez The two series are executive produced by Jimenez and Flavio Morales, who was an EP on HBO Max’s global hit “Like Water for Chocolate.” Sergio Jablon (“Súbete a mi moto”) serves as a writer on both series. “We’ve assembled a tremendous team, both in front of and behind the camera, for these two series and we can’t wait to share them with the ViX audience,” said Jimenez. “Trapped with the Enemy” is described as a “romantic thriller that unfolds in real time, within a single setting, where the suspense offers no respite and desire seeps through the cracks of fear.” It follows Clara, who thought her nightmare was over when her abusive ex, Hugo, is sent to prison. But he’s escaped and is waiting for her in the parking garage after work. With her car sabotaged, no phone signal and a dead guard nearby, escape seems impossible — until Leo appears. Mysterious and eerily like Hugo, he could be her savior or her next threat. As the danger closes in, an unexpected connection sparks. “Threatened Infidelity” is “a romantic comedy with teeth — where infidelity is the doorway into a twisty thriller of entanglements, betrayals and desire, in which no one is entirely innocent… but some are far guiltier than others.” It centers on Daniela, who returns home to find her husband, Mario, secretly having an affair with their yoga instructor neighbor, Valentina. When a forgotten watch exposes him, Daniela finds an unexpected ally in Carlos, the handsome new neighbor. But Valentina’s affair is part of a darker scheme: she wants the building Daniela’s father designed — and she’ll eliminate anyone who stands in her way. Fernanda Romero (“The Eye,” “The Burning Plain”) stars in both microdramas while Suanny Serpas (“Eye for an Eye”) and comedian Concrete also appear in “Threatened Infidelity.” Liliana Arriaga (“La Chupitos”) makes a special appearance in “Trapped with the Enemy.” Launched last year, ViXMicrO features the wildly popular short-form scripted series that are designed for vertical, mobile-first viewing. According to research company Omdia, the format, which first originated in China, generated global revenues of $11 billion last year and is expected to hit $14 billion by the end of 2026, with Latin America emerging as a major market. The format is particularly popular with the youth, with politicians turning to it to power up the youth vote, most recently by L.A. mayoral candidate Nithya Raman. Madrid-based confab Iberseries & Platino Industria, running Sept. 29 – Oct 2, has programmed events around the fast-growing format. Specializing in original series and films in both Spanish and English, JK Media recently launched “Ninel Conde: Sin Filtro” with ViX and produced the historic pay-per-view live broadcast of “Gloria Trevi: Live” from BMO Stadium, which was streamed with VEEPS. title: How a Microdramas Director Landed Her First Feature Film Gig
full_text: × Skip to main content By Katie Kilkenny Plus Icon Katie Kilkenny Enterprise Reporter, TV & Labor katiekilkenny7 Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 7:30am Kristen Brancaccio Chris Jon Directing a microdrama and directing a feature-length film are very different tasks, typically diverging in budgets, schedules and expectations for a viewer’s attention span. But in an era when more up-and-comers and film school grads are going straight into the verticals business, it’s possible that some of Hollywood’s next big feature directors could emerge from the world of bite-sized entertainment. What exactly would that transition look like? Kristen Brancaccio, who The Hollywood Reporter has learned was just tapped by Graviteur Studios to helm its first feature film Crush Party , has a pretty good idea. Related Stories TV 'The Tonight Show' Is Bringing Back Its Billionaire Microdrama Satire for a Second Season Business Microdrama Producers Voice Cautious Optimism on the Sector Despite AI Worries Brancaccio has an impressive resume in the microdrama world. She’s directed 21 verticals, including one bona fide hit in Screen Time , the first microdrama from Issa Rae’s company Hoorae Media, which earned nearly 75 million views in its first week on TikTok and PineDrama. She also directed one of aTwist’s first projects, Hollywood Starlet , produced by The Bold and the Beautiful producer Bradley Bell, and the Audible vertical Southern Belle Insults starring Keke Palmer. That’s not to mention her work on YouTube, which is how Brancaccio broke into the business, working on the comedy channel The Key of Awesome and then as an independent contractor directly for the platform. Crush Party , beginning principal photography in 2027, will be her first-ever feature. For Graviteur Studios development and production head Emerson Davis, Brancaccio’s non-traditional background was a big draw. The indie studio, which launched earlier this year as a joint venture between Dolphin Entertainment and KYNETIC Media Ventures, is focused on creator-driven storytelling at a moment when next-gen directors like Curry Parker and Kane Parsons are burning up the box office. The Graviteur team found Brancaccio through Screen Time , which they enjoyed, later to be impressed by her range as a director. “With Kristen, she’s shown how exceptional of a storyteller she is across formats and genres,” Davis said in an interview. “Some of our early conversations were both about story but a lot about connecting with an audience and what audience are we trying to reach. She brings that natural ability to think like that.” As her journey may — or may not — be a bellwether for promising verticals directors in the future, Brancaccio was game to discuss how it happened. In an interview, she talked about the evolution of the microdrama industry, transferable skills and staying audience-focused in traditional moviemaking. Let’s start with how you got into microdramas in the first place. What led you to the verticals industry? I have a background in the digital space. I started my career on YouTube and over the years have worked on a ton of projects that met where digital and traditional industry converged. And one of the projects that I did was I wrote and directed a pilot for SyFy that was meant to be a digital show. SyFy never ended up going that route, but that pilot ended up with some producers at ReelShort in very early 2024. And it had a very strong romance element and that’s what they were looking for. I got a phone call and they just sort of explained, “Hey, there’s a new format in town. We’re shooting this movie vertically. Are you interested in directing it?” And the rest is history. Do you have any idea how they got their hands on the SyFy pilot? Yes. The production designer from that pilot is friends with a producer from a microdrama production company that was working with ReelShort. So it was just one of those projects that I had written off as a bummer that it never went further than it did, but then ended up totally changing the trajectory of my career path. And I think there were a few reasons they resonated with it. Obviously, the fact that there was romance in this pilot. The budget level was, I would say, comparable to what a lot of microdrama budgets are. And again, it was made for digital, so it moved pretty quickly. I very quickly understood this [microdrama] format. I was like, “Oh, this is for the people. This is what the audience loves. The audience that is reading Wattpad, the audience that is consuming romance, people that just want certain plot points to be hit at a certain speed, people that are addicted to TikTok, they’re expecting a certain cadence and that’s what these shows deliver.” How have you noticed the microdrama industry changing or evolving in particular ways over the last few years? We’re starting to see different lanes emerge. At first, these apps were interchangeable. Now they’re starting to realize the value in building their brand. That’s something that traditional Hollywood players understand very well. And so the people coming into the space like Issa Rae, she knows her audience inside and out, so she’s going to deliver a really compelling, well-told story, perfectly suited for digital, that is going to be high production value. She’s not going to follow the same cadence or rules that ReelShort follows. It’s just a totally different approach, but it’s very, very successful. The one I did for her has at least 250 million views, if not more. And then we’re also seeing a lot of very talented people [that] really understand the audience they’re going for. They’re not ignoring the work that has been done so far in the microdrama space. I think they’re doing a very good job actually of analyzing that, what has worked so far? Why has it worked? What can we do differently? As you’ve been working on all these microdramas, how did the chance to direct this feature come up for you? This is what I was hoping and praying that this corner of the industry would lead to. For a long time, verticals were in this… almost a silo. It was just shoved to the corner. I don’t know if “stigma” is maybe too strong a word, but there wasn’t an understanding that there was value in what we were doing and in the skills that we were developing. I have a background in producing and I was just consistently blown away by frankly what I could accomplish myself, but also what everyone in this corner of the industry is doing. We’re doing so much in such a fast timeline. We’re doing it consistently. We’re turning out a movie a month, essentially. I was like, man, I hope other industry players notice this. It all starts with a phone call coming out of the blue and [I] found out that David and Bill at Graviteur were…. I think it was Screen Time that had caught their eye. They had this movie script that they developed in-house, they were looking for a director and they really saw the value in somebody with vertical experience, somebody that had all those skills that I mentioned, both the technical and the creative, that comes from just working in digital and specifically working in verticals. I was so excited to get that call because I was like, “Oh my gosh, this is everything. This is what I hoped would happen. People are recognizing the value in these skills.” What are some of the lessons that you’ve learned in the microdrama industry that you’re planning on bringing to your work on Crush Party ? I’ve met some very, very talented, skilled people who can accomplish a lot on a limited budget, both in front of the camera and behind the camera, [and I’m] actually wanting to bring some people with me. Aside from that, I think the aspect that I’m going to bring with me to Crush Party and other projects is I feel like I keep the audience in mind in a different way and meet the audience where they are. And what’s nice about this script in particular is it’s targeting an audience that is thriller and horror. Those are emerging genres in the microdrama space and fans are starting to really respond to them. When you’re thinking about the audience, it causes you to think about the whole project in a different way. So many filmmakers forget that you’re making your movie for an audience and you can make the best movie in the world, but if it doesn’t reach the audience, no one’s going to see it and that’s such a shame. So who is your audience? What is it they’re looking for? What matters to them? That needs to matter to you too. On the flip side, are there any elements when it comes to working on a feature that you feel will really stretch you as a director? When you make a lot of microdramas, you understand the time you have and the decisions you make are usually to meet those demands on time and budget. Unfortunately, time, budget, creative is the order in which you have to think about things. It’s a necessity; thinking the opposite way will make you crazy in the microdrama space. But I think it’s going to be a little bit of a brain rearrangement, a very lovely one, to maybe be able to say, okay, obviously this is not a massive budget studio feature, right? So I’m aware of what this budget is and what it can get me, but it does allow me to think creatively first, and then assess, okay, does this work with the time and budget that we have? In general, what kind of preparation do you think microdramas offer early-career directors for working in other formats like features? I think the value in directing microdramas is learning the skill of shooting for the edit. You don’t have time to find the movie in post. So even if you have time on set, which you never do, at the end of the day, these post timelines are so tight, you don’t have time to try and shape it into anything else. And obviously your scripty [script supervisor] is hopefully there to help you, but as a director, you also need to learn that skill. Working with actors, you don’t have time for a ton of takes. So learning very quickly how to communicate to an actor, how to quickly understand maybe why isn’t a scene working or what could we adjust in this scene to make it better or to change the energy of the scene. You get very quick. So I think overall it’s getting your reps in all these different areas. You’re shooting multi-cam, you have to be able to hold in your head what multiple cameras are doing. I think there’s just so much value in the technical, practical skills of directing when you’re directing microdramas. What are your ultimate aspirations as a director and where do you want to go from here? I’m going to sound like a cliché, but I love telling stories. And so I think I’m very interested in telling stories in lots of different mediums, lots of different ways. I don’t know what the future of my career looks like, but I’m pretty confident that it will involve somehow combining my digital experience with narrative experience. And whether that’s in more digitally focused projects or more films or streaming projects, I don’t know. But that seems to be what my career has flirted [with] consistently, at that meeting point. And I think Graviteur has the right idea in that they’re creating a movie that is a very traditional format, but just the fact that they even hired me, they’re thinking about it also with the eye towards what matters in digital, what skills do people coming from digital bring to the table, which is very cool. I think they’re a little ahead of the curve on that. I mean, we’ve obviously also seen many examples of YouTube creators doing this very successfully, but I think that will stop being an outlier and that will start being a more established pipeline. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. THR

Actor and director Eric Stoltz ( Madam Secretary , Nashville ) is directing from a screenplay by Hailey Lustig, founder of Three Birds Landing Productions, and composer Robbie Roth, which takes inspiration from their real lives. Co-writers Lustig and Roth were born in the same Toronto maternity ward on either side of midnight and grew up together at summer camp and have been best friends for decades. Hailey and Robbie have written something funny and deeply personal about friendship, first love, and the lives we choose for ourselves. Robbie’s songs are woven beautifully through that world.” Both Sides Now is independently financed by Three Birds Landing Productions and marks the company’s debut feature film. The film is produced by Lustig, Carrie Mudd and Erin Berry, in association with Peacock Alley Entertainment. Production began September 19 in Muskoka, Ontario, and is scheduled to wrap October 20. Li Plus Icon Jenny S. Li Latest Lee Sinje Readies Feature Directing Debut ‘Wanita,’ Unveils ‘Dead Tide’ at Pingyao 3 hours ago ‘Light Pillar’ Director Xu Zao Readies AI-Themed Follow-Up ‘Easy, My Friend’ 4 hours ago Jia Zhangke Readies Zhao Tao Road Movie ‘Mamma Dunhuang,’ Rules Out AI in Production (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Unknown Pleasures Pictures Jia Zhangke ‘s Unknown Pleasures Pictures has acquired China rights to Apichatpong Weerasethakul ‘s “Jenjira’s Magnificent Dream,” co-founder Tian Qi has confirmed to Variety . The Chinese art-house distributor is also negotiating to acquire two titles from this year’s Cannes Film Festival. In June, it added Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” and Marine Atlan’s “La Gradiva,” and in January it took Greater China rights to Rafael Manuel’s Sundance title “Filipiñana,” which Jia executive produced and which had its Asian premiere at Pingyao this week. Related Stories Tom Hiddleston Recalls Trekking to Everest for ‘Tenzing’ and Kevin Feige Telling Him ‘Thor’ Wasn’t ‘Going to Be the Only Film’ He Would Play Loki In How Oscar-Tipped Rising Star Anthony Ippolito Turned ‘I Play Rocky’ Into ‘I Play Sylvester’: ‘You Only Have One Chance to Do This’ Named after Jia’s 2002 feature, Unknown Pleasures is run by Jia and distributor Tian, who also founded Hero Films, the distributor of Gu You’s Busan title “The First Taste of Loneliness.” The label focuses on niche international art films, and alongside festival titles, it looks for hidden gems that lack strong international sales backing. Popular on Variety Before the label launched, Tian’s previous company released Weerasethakul’s “Memoria” in China, where it grossed $360,000, a third of the film’s total box office. Jia and Tian say that early success gave them confidence. Unknown Pleasures launched in 2025, with Italian director Paola Cortellesi’s “There’s Still Tomorrow,” one of Italy’s biggest box office hits of 2023. Acquired in 2024, the film screened at the Pingyao International Film Festival and opened in Chinese cinemas on March 8 for International Women’s Day. He adds that not every acquisition has to turn a profit. “Once we acquire a title, we definitely aim to release it with the fastest speed.” Jia says he and Tian agree on keeping the company’s finances stable, but the main mission remains “to distribute films we truly like. If we stand purely from a business point, we wouldn’t start this business anyways.” He wants the company to help grow China’s art-film market. “We operate with a long-term library strategy: these titles should remain evergreen in the coming years. By building our own catalog and taking a long-term financial view, we keep the revenue sustainable,” Jia says. For Jia, movies “that are genuinely interesting, deserve to be shared, and people might easily pass over – those are the ones that really need to be seen in a cinema.” “We can’t help but sigh over some films that were released online – they actually belong to cinema,” he says. title: ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Intimate Docuseries Gets Netflix Premiere Date, Trailer
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Intimate Docuseries Gets Netflix Premiere Date, Trailer Broadway-Bound ‘Beat Street’ Musical From Grammy-Winning Rapper Nas Assembles Creative Team ‘School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play’ Broadway Review: When Escape Is Just A Clique Away View All September 29, 2026 7:12am Add us as a Google Preferred Source In the new trailer for Netflix The One About Matthew Perry , the late Friends star reflects on his TV success and the toll it took. In a voiceover early in the clip, Perry says, “I said God, you can do anything you want to me just please make me famous.” When fame arrived, Perry reflected, “God did not forget the other part.” The three-episode series, described by Netflix as “an intimate documentary series exploring the life and legacy of Matthew Perry,” premieres globally on the streamer October 27. Check out the trailer above. Directed by Mary Robertson, the docuseries features interviews with Perry’s family and friends, including sister Mia Perry Bowick, close friends David Pressman and Roger Castillo, former NBC President Warren Littlefield and others who knew or worked with the late Friends star. Related Stories Casting Netflix's 'Women Like Us' Adds Nine To Cast Casting Lindsay Lohan & Henry Golding To Lead Netflix Romantic Feature 'Return To You' From Director Mark Waters The two-minute trailer chronicles Perry’s experience with fame and the realization that it was not actually everything he wanted. Using testimonies from his sister Mia Perry Bowick, several other close friends and unreleased photos and videos from the Perry family’s private archive, the three-part series explores his career as a beloved actor and comedian while also revealing details about his long-term struggle with drug use and his attempts to get sober (he spent more than $7 million in those efforts, the doc says). Watch on Deadline The release of the film comes on the third anniversary of Perry’s death. In a statement accompanying the Netflix premiere date announcement, Perry’s sister said, “It’s taken time for me to feel ready to share these memories and what it was like to love Matthew through all the complexity of his life—to see him as a whole person, not just as Chandler, and not just as someone who struggled with addiction. As his sister, he shaped who I am today, the person I strive to be, and the work to which I’ve devoted my life. “Matthew had a beautiful heart,” she continues, “and a generous spirit, and even in his darkest moments, he could still make you laugh and feel loved. I hope this series gives everyone who loved him, whether personally or from afar, a deeper appreciation for who he truly was, and the legacy he leaves behind.” “Matthew Perry was one of the comedic geniuses of our time,” said director Robertson. “Through his many films, TV and stage performances, and his unforgettable portrayal of Chandler Bing, he made millions of us laugh, connect, and feel a little less alone. He also gave us so much more by bravely speaking about addiction. Yet the public only knew part of his story. That’s why we set out to make this film: to let the people who knew and loved Matthew reveal the person behind the public figure.” Netflix’s The One About Matthew Perry is executive produced by Mary Robertson, Lisa Kalikow, Eli Holzman and Aaron Saidman; co-executive produced by Lora Moftah; and produced by Jessica Call. Maxine Productions, a part of Sony Pictures Television, is the production company. Check out the trailer above. title: Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 29, 2026 7:07am PT Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) By Anna Marie de la Fuente Plus Icon Anna Marie de la Fuente @adelafuente1 Latest Chile’s Sanfic Set to Screen Late Documentarian Antonio Caro’s Swan Song ‘Monguen’ Among Nine Chilean Pics in Competition (EXCLUSIVE) 1 hour ago ‘The Platform’ Co-Producer David Matamoros of Doce Entertainment Spain Boards Matías Rojas’ ‘Dog Legs’ (EXCLUSIVE) 8 hours ago Madrid Audiovisual Cluster Dives Deeper Into New Business Models, AI and Emerging Technologies at Iberseries & Platino Industria 10 hours ago See All 'Monguen' Courtesy of Sanfic Chile’s 22nd Santiago Film Festival ( Sanfic ) features nine pics in its Chile Film Competition this year vying for cash prizes in the best film, director and actor categories. Among them, four are debut features, including “ Erratics” by Thomas Woodroffe, which competed at the San Sebastian Festival’s New Directors sidebar. The lineup also features ‘Monguen,’ the swan song of docu filmmaker Antonio Caro, who died unexpectedly a few weeks ago. “We present his film with special affection, as a way of honoring his work and keeping his perspective present within this selection,” said Sanfic artistic director, Carlos Núñez. Related Stories ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has Already Made $50 Million in Pre-Sales, Three Months Before Release 'Avengers: Endgame Encore' Adds 4 New Scenes Tying to 'Doomsday': [SPOILER] Fights Doctor Doom, [SPOILER] Travels to the Past and the Multiverse Collapses “This competition reflects a particularly diverse moment in Chilean cinema, with films that engage with our present through very different languages, territories and generations. There are works that cross between fiction and documentary, new voices alongside filmmakers with established careers, and a strong presence of perspectives emerging outside traditional centers of production,” he pointed out. Popular on Variety “We want Sanfic to be precisely that kind of space: a place where Chilean cinema can connect with its audiences while, at the same time, reaching an international stage.” Chile’s film industry has never been more robust, with the 2026-2027 industry catalog reporting a 20.5% surge compared to the last season. The catalog was unveiled at the San Sebastián Festival where eight Chilean titles screened across seven sections. However, the industry is bracing for some belt tightening – and will most likely resort to even more co-productions starting next year – given the upcoming cuts announced by the administration of new President Jose Antonio Kast, who took office in March. Cuts to the Ministry of Culture and various competitive funds for the Arts are forthcoming although the ministry downplayed the cutback, stressing that it would be an overall decrease of 9% next year. However, the Audiovisual Investment Support Fund drops from approximately $586,000 (540 million pesos) in 2026 to $208,000 (192 million pesos) in 2027—a 64% reduction. Speaking to Variety when the news first broke, Alejandra Garcia of Ronda Cine, producer of “The Meltdown,” Chile’s Oscars submission, said: “The recent budget cuts to culture in Chile are deeply frustrating. It’s difficult to understand why a country’s support for culture is still seen as an expense to be reduced, rather than an investment that should be strengthened.” The other nine sections of the festival will be announced on Oct. 20. Sanfic runs Nov. 2 – 6 in Santiago de Chile. Chilean Pics in Competition: “Animals” (Andrés Waissbluth Weinstein, Retaguardia Films, Avispa Cine, Frutacina, Chile, Argentina) In a near future where animals have civil rights, three privileged couples see their lives disrupted by an eerily human quadruped: a sheep running for office, a dog that can sniff out lies and a jealous cat. Produced by Felipe Azúa and Iván Eibuszyc, the Chilean-Argentine Sanfic world premiere was developed through Santiago Lab, BrLab and Guadalajara’s Co-production Meeting, with support from CORFO, Ibermedia and Buenos Aires’ Mecenazgo program. ‘Animales’ “Beat” (“Latir,” Patricio Loutit Azócar, Suroeste Films, Reinos Cine, Chile) Loutit Azócar’s feature debut follows Manuel, a retired university professor who joins a body-percussion workshop during Chile’s 2022 constitutional plebiscite. The experience transforms his life as he confronts his wife’s terminal illness. World premiering at Sanfic, it was produced by Manuel González Llanos and Daniel Rebolledo. The Chilean production received support from the Audiovisual Development Fund in 2024 and participated in Industria FIC Viña’s 2024 business meetings. ‘Beat’ “Black Corp,” (“Cuadro Negro,”Carolina Adriazola and José Luis Sepúlveda, Iglo Cine Chile) Adriazola and Sepúlveda’s film follows Sofía, a young journalist documenting the Chilean army who returns to live with her grandmother after a breakup. She meets María, whose view of the military legacy contrasts with her grandmother’s. Produced by Sofía Paloma Gómez, José Luis Sepúlveda and Carolina Adriazola, the film premiered at Punto de Vista, winning the Grand Prize for Best Film and Youth Jury Award for Best Film. It marks its Latin American premiere. ‘Black Corp’ “Death Brought You Back” (“La muerte te vio volver,” Sebastián Cuevas Barria, Praxia Producciones, Mala Films, Chile; Vert & Bleu Productions, France) Cuevas Barria’s debut follows Silvia, returning to Chiloé after 30 years to claim her dying mother’s inheritance and confront a disturbing family past. Produced by Catalina Alarcón Reyes, it received support from Chile’s Audiovisual Fund and was developed through Sanfic Lab, CCC and the Lebu Film Festival Lab. Selected for Sanfic’s 2024 Ibero-American WIP, it won the Films en Cours Award at Entrevues Belfort and FECILS’ Sound Award. Participated in Ventana Sur in Montevideo. ‘Death Brought You Back’ “Erratics” (“Bloques Erráticos,” Thomas Woodroffe , La Belle Affaire Productions, Un Puma, Chile, France, Argentina) Woodroffe’s debut follows filmmaker Lucien Castelnau’s ghost, played by France’s Denis Lavant (“Holy Motors”), released from a glacier after a century into a futuristic Patagonia where technological progress collides with forgotten histories. A Rotterdam CineMart winner produced by Rodrigo Díaz, Pascual Mena and Jérôme Blesson, the Chilean-French-Argentine co-production was developed through La Fabrique Cinéma, TorinoFilmLab, CineMart Darkroom and Sanfic Lab. Selected for San Sebastián’s New Directors , it received Eurimages’ New Lab Outreach Award and support from Chile’s Audiovisual Fund and TorinoFilmLab’s Co-production Fund. ‘Erratics’ “Floating Population” (“Población Flotante,” Carlos Araya Díaz, Maria una vez, Chile) Araya Díaz’s docu-fiction hybrid follows a filmmaker reconnecting with a childhood friend through an actor’s voice, revisiting his final days as a bus worker. World premiered at Czech Republic’s Ji.hlava Fest and marking its Latin American premiere at Sanfic, the film was produced by María Paz González and developed through Encuentros Australes at FIC Valdivia, where it won Best Chilean Film of the Future (First Cut) in 2023, plus WIP selections at FIC Viña del Mar. ‘Floating Population’ “Inner Rebellion” (“Rebelión Interior,” Sofía Paloma Gómez Vergara, La Jauría Comunicaciones, Chile) Gómez Vergara’s documentary revisits Chile’s social uprising through a health brigade treating protesters injured by police repression, connecting present violence with dictatorship-era wounds. World premiering at Sanfic, it was produced by Catalina Alarcón Reyes and developed through FIC Valdivia’s Cine Chileno del Futuro, where it won Best Chilean Film of the Future (Post-production) and the Sonamos Award. It also participated in WIP FicViña, DocsMX and Fidba’s LINK-WIP and received national post-production funding in 2025. ‘Inner Rebellion’ “Monguen” (“Life,” Antonio Caro, Lemuntu Producciones, Totem Producciones, Chile) The late Caro’s documentary feature follows Fresia, a young Mapuche woman from Alto Biobío who must leave her community to give birth in the city, navigating motherhood between two worlds. World premiering at Sanfic, the film is produced by Michel Toledo and was developed through Conecta CCDoc, Residencia Arca, Nuevas Miradas EICTV, Hot Docs Forum, Cannes Docs at Marché du Film and Encuentros Australes Fic Valdivia. “The Tiger of the East” (“El Tigre del Este,” Jorge Acevedo, Yareta Films, Queltehue Films, Chile; Estudio Churubusco, Mexico) Acevedo’s debut pic follows Andrés, a young Chilean muleteer and self-taught musician who leaves his hometown to pursue his dream of becoming a professional musician in Mexico. His wish to gift an original song to Los Tigres del Norte inspires the journey. Produced by Mixie Araya Soler, the Chilean-Mexican co-production premiered at Shanghai Film Festival.
