title: Kyle MacLachlan, Star of David Lynch’s ‘Dune,’ Was the Only One on Set Who Knew What ‘Dune’ Was About
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kyle MacLachlan Plus Icon Kyle MacLachlan View All September 29, 2026 7:00am Kyle MacLachlan as Paul Atreides in 'Dune' (1984), directed by David Lynch. Courtesy Everett Collection Chihuahua, Mexico Spring 1983 Filming out in the Chihuahuan Desert is actually chilly in the morning, but when the sun comes up, the heat is unreal. Just biblical. With the camera crew setting up in the distance and the wind not cooperating, Patrick Stewart and I sweat in our “stillsuits” and wait. In the world of Dune , the suit transforms the sweat into drinking water; but in the Mexican desert, the sweat just pools, sticks to my skin and runs down my arms. The custom-fit suit is a near-torture device of costuming that severely limits my ability to move. It’s like fighting against a giant rubber band wrapped around my body. When the suit is zipped all the way up, I can’t even raise my arms. Not ideal. The key, I’m learning, is to limit unnecessary movement. Or, really, any. Related Stories Movies Naomi Watts Praises Husband Billy Crudup for Backing Her Menopause Activism: "So Sweet -- and Sexy" TV Hints of 'Sex and the City' and 'Narcos': A Look at Literary Works Being Pitched for Screen Adaptations at Iberseries & Platino Industria Wondering how much longer before we roll, I turn to see David Lynch , the film’s director, up on a desert dune in a yellow hat, white collared shirt, the shortest shorts on earth, and brown loafers with white socks pulled up to his knees. (He has a particular distaste for sand in his shoes.) He’s talking to cinematographer Freddie Francis, shirtless in a boater hat, and to the assistant director, José “Kuki” López Rodero, in a white panama hat. They are huddled together around the camera, looking like a bizarre collection of bandits. Freddie’s crew is setting up big silver reflectors to light the actors’ faces, which bounce the sunlight right into our eyeballs. Brutal. (Now I understand why Clint Eastwood characters are always squinting.) In the distance, across the Samalayuca Dune Fields, men are burn­ing old tires to get the right color and intensity of black smoke. As a key point of the plot, the planet Arrakis, aka Dune, doesn’t have water; thus, it has no blue sky. But of course, Mexico does. Can’t get around that. So, our intrepid director, the 37-year-old for­mer Eagle Scout from Montana, the Oscar-nominated visionary be­hind Eraserhead and The Elephant Man, Lynch has taken on the not-inconsiderable task of blotting out the sky. Those tires are still burning in the distance, but now the black smoke is moving in the wrong direction, away from us. So, we wait. We can blot out the sky, rip up the desert, but we can’t control which way the wind blows. Assuming it’ll be some time, I unzip my stillsuit to down around my torso and tie the arms around my waist, my black T-shirt comically drenched: I’m now half Paul, half Kyle. Both of us carrying a lot on our minds — and shoulders. Kyle Maclachlan ‘s memoir, Fictional Selves (Crown). Penguin Random House Dune is populated by an impressive list of international talent on and off camera: acclaimed actors like Max von Sydow, Francesca Annis, Jürgen Prochnow; up-and-comers like Blade Runner ’s Sean Young and gigantic stars like Sting; top craftsmen like Oscar-winning cinematographer Freddie Francis, Tony Masters (Stanley Kubrick’s production designer), effects wizard Kit West ( Raiders of the Lost Ark ), creature creator Carlo Rambaldi (who also designed E.T.), and famed costume designer Bob Ringwood, whose Batman suit five years later will be modeled on the “fetish industrial” look of Dune ’s rubber stillsuits. In Mexico for budgetary reasons, the day-to-day production has customs issues, technology issues, communication issues, construction issues, electricity issues, on top of the typical challenges that come with a movie of this size and complexity. The power goes out regularly — our home base, Mexico City, has brownouts — and the crew on the soundstages often have to switch to generators. It’s a real roll-with-the-punches situation, an adventure in the grandest sense of the word. When I first arrive, I am wide-eyed, viewing the project as a throwback to the “sword and sandal” movies of the 1950s and early ’60s that I used to watch on TV. Go off somewhere impossible and exotic and come back and hope you have a movie. During the scene Patrick Stewart and I are shooting that day, Paul Atreides, the character I play, has been in the desert for a couple of years. I had petitioned for my hair to go past my shoulders, Jesus style — a sexier and messiah-like Paul — but was overruled. The final decision is a compromise that serves neither side: hair extensions glued to my scalp with a latex adhesive. Taking them off at the end of each day is a painful process that involves rubbing alcohol and a light scalping that leaves behind stubborn balls of latex in my hair. Currently, I am wearing a white hairnet over my perm, to keep it in place before we shoot. Patrick, mostly bald on top, has longer hair extensions, too, given that his character, Paul’s adviser and friend Gurney Halleck, has been in exile as well. We stare off into the distance, catching our breath, saving our energy. The first thing I noticed when I met Patrick was his voice. I went to school for three years to learn how to speak onstage, but I’ll never sound like him. Coming from the prestigious Royal Shakespeare Company, Patrick has the most mellifluous tones, regal and elegant. No one can make the line “Behold, as a wild ass in the desert go I forth to my work” sound correct except for him. He is Gurney Halleck, master swordsman and troubadour. And because he’s also Patrick Stewart, he’s suave and debonair about it. When he puts on the Atreides battle jacket or the Fremen stillsuit, it’s like he’s lived in it all his life. He also has the most marvelously shaped head of any human I’ve ever seen, and I tell him so. He gives me a “thank you, I think” kind of look. Patrick is in his early 40s at the time, but this is only his third film, and he’s a neophyte when it comes to the complicated world of Dune. Because he’s a last-minute replacement — for Aldo Ray, whose struggles with alcoholism have rendered him out of commission — I try to offer assistance. Patrick simply hasn’t had time to soak up the extensive Dune lore I have spent a lifetime accumulating. Still, we are both newcomers to film, so we share a certain awe about the hectic and bizarre world spinning around us. MacLachlan (left), Patrick Stewart (center) and Sting (knife), in Dune . Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection Patrick is a mix of stately confidence and thoughtful inquiry. He regularly leans over and, sotto voce , asks me questions about what’s going on. Though he presents a very cool and collected mien, he is just trying to figure shit out like me. We connect on our theater background — I did Shakespeare the previous summer — and laugh at the exponential difference between simple theater productions and … whatever this is. The size and scope of the film often leave us speechless, and I feel less alone with him beside me. On his first day of shooting, he and I took our seats in a half-built “ornithopter,” which is like a giant, multifaceted bee that flies over the desert. We were seated in front of a gigantic blue screen, where the landscape would be matted in later. I could feel Patrick’s nervousness as we prepared to “fly” over the shield wall and the Great Desert of Arrakis. He leaned forward and quietly asked, “Kyle, what are we looking at here?” I leaned back and spoke in an undertone: “There’s a sandworm down there bigger than a tractor trailer.” “Aha. And there?” he asked, pointing lower down. “It’s swallowing one of the harvesters.” “Harvester?” he asked. “It’s like a large metal factory on wheels.” “Seems like a risky mission,” he said, a trace of somber gravitas. “Tremendous risk,” I said quietly. Patrick’s key line in the scene is “The worm is eight minutes away, sire.” After the first take, he had a question. “Pardon, David?” “YES, PATRICK,” David said in his distinctive honk. “How exactly would I know how far out the worm is?” I’m impressed that Patrick exists deeply enough within his character to ask such a thing. David stopped, re-calculating in his mind. “EXCELLENT QUESTION, PATRICK,” he said, like a supportive teacher. “THANK YOU.” He then dispatched a propman to construct a gauge, with analog hands to be inserted later. Having carried the world of Dune in my head for years, I, too, arrived on set with such inquiries. Carefully and diplomatically, I at first pushed back on some production details. I know the book inside and out — I am likely the only one on set who does — so I feel I carry a responsibility to the story. When I was fitted for the stillsuit, I felt some things were missing: “How come these suits don’t have hoods?” “Where are the capes?” “Will there be a headpiece?” “Wait, where’s the mouthpiece so you don’t lose moisture when you breathe?” I wasn’t trying to be difficult; it’s just that I had absorbed the reality of Frank Herbert’s story so completely. If Paul had to survive in that desert climate, in those bleak conditions, with only this protection, he would die. And if being stranded on Dune wasn’t a life-or-death situation, then that would change a whole series of things that affected the characters’ decisions. There was an internal logic that needed to remain intact. My concerns were never about my ego or vanity, but about the truth of that world. “Kale,” said producer Dino De Laurentiis, still struggling to pronounce my name. “We don’t hire famous actors to cover their faces where no one can see them.” This did have an unavoidable logic to it. He had plenty to worry about already, and often he and his daughter Raffaella De Laurentiis, also a producer on the film, and David were managing a hundred things at once on a scale I couldn’t even conceive. After my third degree about the costume, I made a point to choose my battles more carefully. Still standing around in the broiling desert with Patrick, waiting for the smoke to change direction, we walk over to where Everett McGill is sitting on a chair beneath umbrellas, out of the sun. Everett, who plays Stilgar, a tribal leader of the indigenous “Fremen,” has the calm but commanding presence of an Old West sheriff. He’s got classic movie-star features, a strong jaw and penetrating eyes, but he remains offbeat enough to stay interesting. “Hey, young buck,” Everett says, his nickname for me. “Surviving?” I part my hands, like Take a look , making a dramatic flourish of my current state — hairnet, half-removed stillsuit, sweat-drenched T-shirt. Everett is a different breed of actor, and I’m instantly drawn to him. He’s a taciturn guy who grew up in Kansas, and he has that cowboy feel about him, even down to his badass boots, which I make sure to find a pair of for myself. To protect his vocal cords, he carries a converted soda bottle from which he regularly inhales. It is lined with damp cotton, to hold moisture. He wants Stilgar’s voice to have the deep timbre of a respected elder. Everett is meticulous and thorough, if eccentric, carefully considering all kinds of little details for his character. Patrick, Everett, and I stare at the thick black smoke coming off the burning tires, the most toxic cloud I’ve ever seen. “You think that’s why we couldn’t shoot this in the States?” I ask, and Patrick and Everett laugh. Everett seems more sanguine about our current conditions. He’s been around. “This is child’s play,” he says, “compared to what we went through on Quest. ” He has been entertaining us with tales from Quest for Fire, the historical fantasy film directed by Jean-Jacques Annaud that he recently made with Ron Perlman and Rae Dawn Chong. The film had a legendary shoot, nearly a year long: actors sitting for five hours of makeup a day, learning a completely invented language, dealing with the elements in freezing Scotland and blistering Kenya. “It was grueling,” Everett says, carefully inhaling from his bottle and regaling us like a chieftain before a campfire. He starts enumerating on his fingers. “Ron and I both got frostbite, they had real bears and elephants on set, a volcano eruption we had to plan around, and a set designer got anthrax from animal skins.” He says it all matter-of-factly, a little pride in his resonant voice. “Jesus,” I say. I glance over at Patrick, and he looks mystified . But as a Hollywood veteran, Everett takes things in stride. Assuming the Dune pictures will keep me in the space-fantasy business for a while — after all, I had signed an enormous book of a contract for five Dune (and three non- Dune ) films for Dino’s company — I listen to his stories in a little bit of awe. I’m excited, even gung ho about clawing my way through those kinds of challenges. The exuberance and stupidity of youth have me embracing the idea of testing myself on a film set. I can’t wait to come back with stories. “Yeah, we kept it light, though,” Everett says. “You gotta. Or you’d go insane. Ron and I were always pulling shit on each other. One time, I had to traverse this sandhill barefoot where the ground temperature was nearly a hundred fifty degrees. When it was Ron’s turn, I waved him up without saying a word, and boy he nearly killed me. The bottoms of his feet were bright red! Nearly scorched them off!” Everett laughs aloud in his rich tenor. Between him and Patrick, I’m surrounded by the most melodious sounds. The three of us are becoming fast friends, and though I’m over a decade younger, I feel comfortable with the relaxed camaraderie in the midst of the madness. I’m discovering that friends on a shoot can become a type of family. We few, we happy few, we band of brothers. Everett is playfully envious of my youth — that’s what the whole “young buck” thing is about. “You gotta get out there and graze, ” he tells me. “Everything is out there for you. You can go all night, come to set without sleeping.” I find his words equally inspiring and demoralizing. I’m not great at embracing the moment and a little gun-shy about real-life adventure. But I have always wanted to traverse the country on a motorcycle; for some reason, after time with Everett, I will make a plan to do exactly that when the shoot ends. It goes against all my natural caution, so it is perfect. Suddenly, the wind shifts. Now the black smoke is blowing right across our faces; it is pure poison, lethal in our throats and lungs, a shock to breathe in. It’s like a neck punch, freezing my vocal cords, stopping me from speaking. Again, not ideal. Everett puts his head down and inhales from his bottle. The rest of us just have to breathe as little as possible. “OKAY, EVERYONE.” David’s distinctive honk comes through nearby walkie-talkies. “GET IN POSITION, PLEASE.” Extras spread out across the dunes. Crew members scurry over to the actors with a gardening-type tool, opening the nozzle and blowing a cloud of yellow and red dust onto us. I close my eyes as it covers my hair and face, hold my breath as it gets up my nose and the grit lodges in my teeth. “BOBBY,” David says over the walkie. “WILL YOU HIT KYLE ONE MORE TIME?” Someone from wardrobe runs over and shoots me with the dirt gun again for good measure. Now I’m completely covered in it. When I turn around and face the camera, I notice that every single crew member is wearing a nose mask, face covering, and giant black-framed goggles. I have to keep from laughing. The “dirt” is actually a calcium-based clay called fuller’s earth, a powder that gives images texture and a sense of depth. The effects team has set giant airplane propeller–type fans right off camera. During the shot, they feed fuller’s earth into the fan blades to be blown onto the actors. When I get home that night, I’ll have to rinse out my teeth, spitting red-dirt saliva into the sink. The epitome of Hollywood glamour, just like Cary Grant. I get into position, the fans blowing dirt and smoke across my face. We spent hours waiting for the wind and then create our own. This is madness. This is Dune. Paul’s costume includes a “weirding module” attached to his throat; it sticks out like a giant door hinge. In the scene, he and Gurney recognize each other in the desert after years apart, a heartwarming moment. But as he hugs me, Patrick accidentally jabs the module back into my Adam’s apple. I am stunned as my breath and voice stop sharply. My eyes fill with tears from the pain, and I make a slight grunting sound. I don’t speak because I can’t. The wind shifts again right as we finish, so that’s the take that goes into the film. Moving on. Excerpted from FICTIONAL SELVES: A Memoir by Kyle MacLachlan. Copyright © 2026 by Kyle MacLachlan. Classic ‘Document’ In Full ASIFA-Showcase Set For November, New FYC Event From Annie Awards Group 2026 Premiere Dates For New & Returning Series On Broadcast, Streaming & Cable View All September 29, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Michael Shannon, left, and Jason Narducy onstage Hard to believe it was 15 years ago last week that R.E.M. called it a career, but fans can re-live the group’s pre-breakout fifth album played in its entirety next year. Oscar nominee Michael Shannon , Jason Narducy and their band are hitting the road again in 2027 to track one of the revered American group’s albums all the way through for its 40th anniversary. Next year’s model is Document, which featured the breakthrough single “The One I Love” and iconoclastic classic “It’s the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine).” Related Stories News R.E.M. Plays First Public Performance In Years At Songwriters Hall Of Fame Induction MTV VMAs 2026 Red Carpet: Taylor Swift, Lisa, Sombr, Charli XCX & More Running from February 3-May 15, the 2027 jaunt spans 27 dates — five more than last year — across 23 cities. Check out the tour schedule below. After running through Murmurs in 2023 and Fables of the Reconstruction and Lifes Rich Pageant the past two years, Shannon, Narducy and company are tackling the first R.E.M. to make the Top 10 and to be certified platinum. Along with its aforementioned two most famous cuts, Document features such often-overlooked gems as “Finest Worksong,” “Oddfellows Local 151,” “Disturbance at the Heron House” and the ever-relevant “Welcome to the Occupation” and “Exhuming McCarthy.” Watch on Deadline The group also will perform many other R.E.M. songs, usually close to 30 each night. “This is the album that introduced me to the band,” Shannon said of Document aka R.E.M. No. 5 , which made Rolling Stone ‘s 2003 list of 500 Greatest Albums of All Time. “If you had told me when I was a kid that some day Iʼd get up on stage and perform it, I wouldnʼt be able to comprehend, probably even believe, that. … Feels like it was recorded yesterday to address the calamity of tomorrow.” Shannon has scored two Supporting Actor Oscar nominations — for 2016’s Nocturnal Animals and 2008’s Revolutionary Road — and a 2023 Emmy nom for his lead role as George Jones in George & Tammy. He also won a pair of Actor Awards (then SAG Awards) for HBO’s Boardwalk Empire. His acting chops are on display when he inhabits R.E.M. frontman Michael Stipe onstage, replicating his singular voice and captivating mannerisms and quirks. Narducy has played with such acts as Bob Mould, Supoerchunk and Sunny Day Real Estate. They’ll be joined on tour by Jon Wurster (drums), John Stirratt (bass), Dag Juhlin (guitar) and Vijay Tellis-Nayak (keyboards). The 2026 tour saw Stipe sing with Shannon and Narducy’s group in Brooklyn and guitarist Peter Buck and bassist Mike Mills join for two shows in R.E.M.’s hometown of Athens, GA. title: YouTube Exec Sees More ‘Obsession’-, ‘Backrooms’-Style Smashes Hitting Box Office – and Oscars
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 29, 2026 6:16am Inde Navarrette and Michael Johnston in 'Obsession.' Courtesy of Focus Features Curry Barker’s Obsession and Kane Parsons’ Backrooms , two Gen Z creatives-led horror stories, have proven the concept that viral online video creators can conquer the box office. And Pedro Pina , vp, YouTube , Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), thinks that they will be followed by more successful moves from the online into the cinema world. He shared that forecast on the opening day of the sixth edition of Iberseries & Platino Industria in Spain’s capital, Madrid , on Tuesday in a keynote appearance entitled “YouTube: The Strategic Ally of the Audiovisual System.” “We can see that creators are defining and shaping the culture. As a result, the cultural impact that we have is phenomenal,” Pina touted. “And you also see, from a cinema standpoint, a huge impact. [The creators of] Obsession and Backrooms , as you know, were YouTubers who decided to go into the box office [business] … – and they were a tremendous success this year. And I would expect to see more and more of these examples [at] the Emmys and Oscars” in the coming years. Pina on Tuesday also explained YouTube’s recent focus on positioning itself as a partner to media and entertainment content companies. “The objective of being here at this event, as well as so many others … is to really show up and really explain how our model works,” he highlighted. “The majority of people in the industry, unfortunately, don’t understand it as much, and that’s 100 percent our fault. We never spent enough time explaining to the industry how we work, how you can monetize.” The result? “To a point, a lot of people were afraid of YouTube. They had fear of YouTube mostly because they did not understand how the platform works, how their content could be protected, how it could reach new audiences, and why it works to monetize,” Pina continued. “Once you start breaking down that information and providing examples and showing the way, you see more and more people starting to look at this. So we started this journey roughly three years ago.” And YouTube has seen the benefit of making its narrative heard. “The amount of content uploaded by traditional players is increasing now,” Pina concluded. Earlier in the Iberseries day, Amazon MGM Studios executives discussed the success of the Mercedes Ron young adult novel adaptations and Spanish zombie horror film Apocalypse Z , while Parrot Analytics shared data trends and estimates for the subscriber impact of Netflix’s Argentina hit series The Eternaut . The industry gathering runs through Friday. THR

title: Amsterdam’s IDFA Adds Ava DuVernay’s ‘14th,’ Laura Poitras’ ‘They’re Here’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All September 29, 2026 6:00am Ava DuVernay with sitting Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden while making '14th.' Paul Garnes/Netflix The 2026 International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam ( IDFA ), which takes place Nov. 12-22, has added more than 100 films to its program, including in its IDFA Competition for Short Documentary. The Dutch doc fest has also added to its Best of Fests, Signed and Paradocs programs, while unveiling first projects for its new media program DocLab. The IDFA Competition for Short Documentary “celebrates the versatility of the form, with 15 films that use creativity and imagination to push the boundaries of short documentary,” organizers said on Tuesday. “Together, they form a mosaic of styles, themes, and perspectives, driven by ambitious directors with singular cinematic voices and strong artistic visions.” Related Stories Business Amazon MGM Execs Tout New Mercedes Ron Hit, How Spain's 'Apocalypse Z' Became a Hit That's Getting a Sequel: "Zombies Have No Nationality" TV Netflix's 'The Eternaut' Effect: Subscriber Impact Estimate Disclosed at Iberseries Among the titles are a tragicomic portrait of humanity and its fallibility, The Bus of Broken Hearts by Björn Carlberg and Johan Palmgren, which follows the world’s biggest cross-country ski race, where thousands of disheartened participants fail to make it to the finish line. Several titles turn their attention to the act of looking itself, including Perihan Incegöz’s Our Village From the Moon , set in the aftermath of an earthquake in southern Turkey, and PICNIC – In Light Invisible to the Human Eye by Jan Ijäs, which “follows Israeli tourists who travel to the border of Gaza to make a spectacle of the devastation of the Palestinian people.” ‘Our Village From the Moon,’ courtesy of IDFA IDFA DocLab, in its 20th anniversary edition, will feature two films that the Netherlands Film Fund and IDFA DocLab have selected for the 2026 Film Fund DocLab Interactive Grant: The Love Files by Sanne De Wilde and Samir Veen, which invites audiences to step inside and critically review a “love file” application for a residence permit, and All the Downtime by Ant Hampton, immersing audiences in an algorithm-led distribution center, just as a power outage disrupts the order and gives way for creative disorder. Also set for the IDFA DocLab and Tamara Shogaolu’s The Invisible Woman , a VR opera that recovers the story of Francisca de Angola, a 17th-century Black woman in Amsterdam, and Polymorf ’s Microbiome Restaurant, with two sensory experiences exploring the human body as an ecosystem. Other projects include Orgasmagoria and Archive Arcade . Signed “showcases the latest cinematic adventures of some of the most original filmmakers of our time,” and its selection of films “celebrates those with a unique artistic signature, beyond the canon,” IDFA highlighted. “The selection reflects on lives lost, those left behind, and what remains after upheaval.” Among this year’s Signed films are Michal Marczak’s Closure , following a father in search of his missing son along the Vistula River near Warsaw, Ava DuVernay’s 14th , tracing the legacy of the U.S. Constitution’s 14th Amendment, Guillaume Massart’s Detention , about a French prison officers’ training school, and They’re Here by Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller, an account of the show of force by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Minneapolis. And in Wild Asparagus , Avi Mograbi returns to his archives of a visit to Palestinian village Saffuriya with his friend Ali Al-Azhari, giving new meaning to decades-old footage. Meanwhile, IDFA’s Best of Fests section will present 59 titles spanning diverse styles and genres and engaging with some of the world’s most pressing topics. Among them are Pegah Ahangarani’s Rehearsals for a Revolution , Ahmed Hassouna’s Citizen Osama , Lukas Marxt’s >1.5°C: Pyropolitics and the New World , The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer by Alessandra Sanguinetti, and Concrete Land by Asmahan Bkerat. Paradocs, in which visual artists and filmmakers present their explorations in non-fiction filmmaking, will this year feature 16 titles exploring the world “through bold formal experimentation, genre-bending, and unexpected perspectives,” Amsterdam organizers said. “A hedonistic escape to a melting glacier is interrupted by apocalyptic climate change and existential anxiety in Susanne Regina Meures’s Eternity – adapting Florentina Holzinger’s performance art to the screen. In The Case Against Space , Graeme Arnfield offers a reconstruction of the first ‘strike’ in space, reframing the astronaut hero through a critical lens on capitalism and surveillance.” Also, Johann Lurf’s Forever…Forever presents a vision of the cosmos in motion, with an ever-accelerating timelapse of the sun’s path filmed over 22 months. Plus, Ãsheghetam by Filmsaaz blends computer animation, fiction, and documentary in a kaleidoscopic portrait of queer love in Tehran, while in Together , ecofeminist art collective Neozoon uses archival and social media footage to explore the tension between communal life and the desire for private property. title: PGA Tour Taps Ryan Holcomb to Lead Original Content (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 6:00am Ryan Holcomb Courtesy of the PGA Tour The PGA Tour is pushing further into entertainment, bringing on Ryan Holcomb to serve as the golf organizer’s senior VP and head of original content. Holcomb was most recently head of development at Box to Box Films, the studio behind shows like Formula 1: Drive to Survive and Faceoff: Inside the NHL , and previously worked in content at World Surf League, Excel Sports Management, STX Entertainment and Lionsgate. At the PGA Tour he will be tasked with helping to develop and drive the Tour’s content beyond the live competitions, including through its PGA Tour Studios content team. Holcomb will report to Luis Goicouria, executive VP & GM of PGA Tour Studios. Holcomb joins the Tour as it leans farther into media, both on and off the course. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp, who previously led the NFL’s media business, is overhauling the structure of the Tour’s events with future media deals in mind. Rolapp’s media background has been useful as the Tour seeks new ways to engage with fans through premium programming. At the same time, there is a growing awareness that other forms of content are needed to help grow fandom around the sport. That’s where PGA Tour Studios and its original content come into focus, with originals and co-productions like Full Swing , Chasing Sunday , and Truth or Putt . PGA Tour Studios sits within the Tour’s enterprise operations division, led by president Andy Weitz, alongside marketing, technology, investor relations and board administration. “The PGA Tour provides an unmatched opportunity to tell stories that deepen the connection between fans and players, while highlighting the incredible competition that defines this sport,” said Holcomb in a statement. “I’m excited to help build on that foundation by developing original content that showcases the personalities, competition and culture of golf in new and compelling ways, reaching audiences wherever they engage with sports and entertainment.” THR

title: ‘SNL UK’ Season 2: All the Hosts and Musical Guests
full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All September 29, 2026 6:00am Danny Dyer, James Norton and Cynthia Erivo will host 'SNL UK' next month. Michael Shelford/Getty Logo text Saturday Night Live UK is back on our screens. The second season kicked off on Saturday, Sept. 9 with host Jeff Goldblum and musical guest CMAT. It follows a well-received first season for SNL UK (a round-up of the reviews can be found here ), which aired from March onwards earlier this year. The series regulars were all relatively unknown stand-up comedians and social media stars, such as Hammed Animashaun, Ayoade Bamgboye, Larry Dean, Celeste Dring, George Fouracres, Annabel Marlow, Al Nash, Jack Shep and Emma Sidi. Weekend Update presenters Ania Magliano and Paddy Young saw particular breakout success, and both of them scored sold-out runs for their solo comedy shows at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival just last month. Related Stories Business Amazon MGM Execs Tout New Mercedes Ron Hit, How Spain's 'Apocalypse Z' Became a Hit That's Getting a Sequel: "Zombies Have No Nationality" TV Netflix's 'The Eternaut' Effect: Subscriber Impact Estimate Disclosed at Iberseries Joining the cast this season is Freddie Meredith, who most recently featured in Kat Sadler’s twisted female-driven comedy Such Brave Girls on the BBC. Season one’s inaugural host was U.S. star and SNL hall-of-famer Tina Fey, who shepherded the show to a solid start. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s review determined : “Good cast, spotty writing — like the mothership,” about the London spin-off of Lorne Michaels’ long-running NBC sketch show. That first episode on Sky (available on Peacock in the U.S.) was watched by over 220,000 people in Britain, as Jamie Dornan, Riz Ahmed, Jack Whitehall, Nicola Coughlan, Aimee Lou Wood, Hannah Waddingham and Ncuti Gatwa booked season one hosting slots. Some of the group’s best sketches across the season included a spoof skincare advert where the women look so young that their partners were arrested for being paedophiles, a Traitors parody whereby a giant crab goes undetected at the roundtable in a savvy social satire, and “The Prince Andrew Plan,” which saw MI5 staffers confirm that every single royal family snafu over the last three decades has all just been to make King Charles look great in comparison. Season two opened with Goldblum and Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, before actor-comedian Jamie Demetriou took the next hosting gig on Sep. 19, with rock band Royal Blood as his musical guest. Demetriou is best known for roles in Fleabag , Stath Lets Flats and Barbie . The following week, Chicken Shop Date presenter Amelia Dimoldenberg took the reins alongside English singer Rachel Chinouriri. Dimoldenberg’s SNL UK appearance came hot on the heels of her confirmation that she’s bringing Chicken Shop Date to an end after 12 years. On Tuesday, Sept. 29, the SNL UK team confirmed the next three hosts: Danny Dyer ( Rivals ) with musical guest Sasha Keable (Oct. 10), James Norton ( House of the Dragon ) and The Streets (Oct. 17), and after that, Cynthia Erivo ( Wicked ) with Blossoms (Oct. 24). On the production side, Laura Claxton has been promoted to SNL UK co-head writer, joining existing head writer Jonno Johnson. Liz Clare returns as director. Heather MacVean joins as costume designer and Sinead Oldnall is heading up the U.K. talent team as director of on-screen talent. Lorne Michaels serves as executive producer on the show, and James Longman is lead producer. Here, THR rounds up the hosts and musical guests confirmed for season two of SNL UK . title: Broadway-Bound ‘Beat Street’ Musical From Grammy-Winning Rapper Nas Assembles Creative Team
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg ‘The One About Matthew Perry’ Intimate Docuseries Gets Netflix Premiere Date, Trailer Broadway-Bound ‘Beat Street’ Musical From Grammy-Winning Rapper Nas Assembles Creative Team Taylor Swift’s “Patient Zero” Music Video Drops: Watch It On Apple Music, Amazon Music Or Spotify View All September 29, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Nas, Schele Williams, Kristoffer Diaz, Jason Michael Webb Production EXCLUSIVE: Beat Street , the Broadway -bound musical based on the groundbreaking 1984 film, has assembled its principal creative team, with The Wiz ‘s Schele Williams , Hell’s Kitchen ‘s Kristoffer Diaz and music supervisor Jason Michael Webb joining the previously announced Nas on the project. Nas, the Grammy-winning, multi-platinum rapper, is creating new material for the production and expanding the film’s soundtrack. Beat Street was one of the first films to depict hip-hop culture, including breakdancing, mixing, scratching, and graffiti art. The film has been cited for its influence by such artists as Ice-T, Ice Cube, LL Cool J and Lin-Manuel Miranda, among many others. Related Stories News 'School Girls; Or, The African Mean Girls Play' Broadway Review: When Escape Is Just A Clique Away Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More Williams will direct the musical, with Diaz writing the show’s book, based upon the MGM Motion Picture. Webb (Broadway’s Choir Boy, MJ: The Musical and the upcoming Purple Rain ) joins the team as music supervisor, arranger, and orchestrator. Watch on Deadline Last month, Nas, Williams, Diaz and Webb collaborated on a 29-hour workshop to develop the stage adaptation. Further details concerning casting and production timeline will be announced in the coming months. Set in the early 1980s, Beat Street revolves around a group of aspiring young talents in the South Bronx, including a graffiti artist, a DJ, and a break-dancer, as they pursue their dreams in the emerging hip-hop scene while facing the challenges of urban life. The film was also notable for appearances by major artists of the era, including Doug E. Fresh, DJ Kool Herc, Afrika Bambataa & The Sonic Force, Us Girls, The Treacherous Three, Magnificent Force, The New York City Breakers, Rock Steady Crew, and Grandmaster Melle Mel & The Furious Five, among others. It was produced by Harry Belafonte and David V. Picker, with music by Belafonte and Arthur Baker, story by Steven Hager, screenplay by Andrew Davis, David Gilbert & Paul Golding, and directed by Stan Lathan, Beat Street starred Rae Dawn Chong, Gus Davis, and Jon Chardiet. Beat Street on Broadway will be produced by Richard Fearn, Arthur Baker, Michael Holman, and Peter Bittenbender, in association with Mass Appeal. Baker and Holman were producers on the original 1984 film. The wildly successful Beat Street soundtrack, released in two volumes, was produced by Baker, with Volume One cited as one of the first rap albums to be certified gold. ShowTown Theatricals will serve as General Managers. Nathan Gehan and Jamison Scott of ShowTown Productions are executive producers of Beat Street. Ascent’s leadership team will span the U.S. and U.K., with Frank Balkin, Molly Bruns, Bill Dispoto, Brian Goldberg, Steve Jacob, Trevor Kossack and Erin Searcy on the West Coast; Juanita Tiangco on the East Coast; and Barnaby Laws, Estere Sulca and Amber Thompson in the U.K. Agent Miranda Roseman joins the agency’s West Coast office.
